title: China–Singapore Naval Cooperation
dek: What official Chinese and Singaporean publications establish about the two navies’ cooperation since 2015, and where that record stops.
research_question: How is China–Singapore naval cooperation evolving, and what does the public record establish about its scope, depth, and limits?

scope.included: Thirteen publications preserved in IPR’s record from August–October 2026 and nine linked official pages from 2015–2024: Singapore MINDEF releases, a parliamentary reply and a factsheet, PLA Daily reports, China defence ministry statements and one Xinhua report.
scope.excluded: Unpublished activity, media and think-tank commentary, coast guard and non-naval cooperation, photographs and any claim to an exhaustive survey of either government’s reporting.
scope.method: Compare dated official accounts edition by edition. Event dates stay distinct from publication dates, and plans stay distinct from reported execution. Chinese evidence is read in the original. Linked pages outside the record are cited by publisher, date and link only.
scope.collection_limits: The record covers recent months; earlier editions rely on linked official pages checked on October 26, 2026 and not preserved by IPR. No paid model processing was used. Restricted source text is not reproduced.

overview: The public record shows one recurring bilateral exercise, Maritime Cooperation, held five times: in 2015 and then every year from 2023 to 2026, with the host alternating since 2023. Official accounts list more activities over time, but Singapore sent one or two ships to each edition whose participants are named. Around the exercise sit routine technical port stops, multinational cadet events and ministerial meetings. China describes deepening cooperation; Singapore presents one partnership among many. The record is official self-description. It does not establish interoperability, readiness or strategic alignment.

sections.heading: Five editions, one interrupted series
sections.intro: The core of the public record is a single bilateral naval exercise, Maritime Cooperation. Official releases document five editions. Counting them from 2015 hides an eight-year gap.

claims.text: MINDEF reported the inaugural edition in Singapore on May 20 and May 23–25, 2015. Singapore sent RSS Intrepid and RSS Valiant; the PLA Navy sent the frigate Yulin.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s May 25, 2015 release gives the shore and sea dates of the first edition.

claims.limits: This is Singapore’s official account. It is the only 2015 publication reviewed here; no Chinese account of the first edition was checked.
claims.heading: 2015: the inaugural edition in Singapore

claims.text: A May 2019 MINDEF release said another edition was planned for 2020. None of the publications reviewed here records that a 2020 edition took place.
claims.limits: A plan is not execution. Finding no record of a 2020 edition here does not prove that it was cancelled or that it did not happen.
claims.heading: A 2020 edition was planned

claims.text: MINDEF announced the second edition for April 28 to May 1, 2023, eight years after the first.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s April 28, 2023 release announced the exercise window on its first day.

claims.limits: The dates come from a release issued on the opening day. This dossier did not review a closing release for the 2023 edition, so the dates are the announced plan.
claims.heading: 2023: the second edition, eight years later

claims.text: MINDEF announced the third edition for September 1–5, 2024 at Zhanjiang. China’s defence ministry described it as the first edition held in China.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s August 29, 2024 release gave the window in advance; China’s ministry described the exercise as it began.

claims.limits: The window comes from releases issued before or during the exercise. Both ministries describe their own exercise; neither is an independent observer.
claims.heading: 2024: the first edition held in China

claims.text: MINDEF announced the fourth edition for May 9–16, 2025. Singapore sent the frigate RSS Steadfast and the mine countermeasures vessel RSS Bedok.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s May 9, 2025 release announced the window on its first day.

claims.limits: This is a release from the opening day. No closing release and no Chinese account of the 2025 edition were reviewed.
claims.heading: 2025: the fourth edition

claims.text: The fifth edition was held at Zhanjiang in September 2026. Each side sent one frigate: RSS Steadfast and the PLA Navy’s Dali. China’s defence ministry dates it September 3–9; MINDEF gives September 5–9. The exercise case study examines that difference.

event_period.date_basis: The ministries agree on a September 9 end but differ on the start: China’s defence ministry gives September 3 and MINDEF September 5.

claims.limits: These are official accounts. The two starting dates are preserved rather than reconciled; the case study sets out what each source does and does not explain.
claims.heading: 2026: the fifth edition, at Zhanjiang

claims.text: Singapore describes the 2026 exercise as the fifth edition conducted since 2015. The record supports that count, but four of the five editions fall in 2023–2026. Annual exercising dates from 2023, not 2015.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s reading of the dated releases. It rests on official counts and on the editions found here; a missing 2020 record does not settle what happened that year.
claims.heading: “Since 2015” hides an eight-year gap

claims.text: Since 2023 the host has alternated each year: Singapore in 2023, Zhanjiang in 2024, Singapore in 2025 and Zhanjiang in 2026. Before the 2024 edition, China’s defence ministry stated an aim of a regular mechanism with hosts alternating annually.
claims.limits: Four years make a pattern, not a commitment. China’s ministry stated an aim; this dossier found no published bilateral agreement that fixes the arrangement, and no Singaporean statement of the same aim was reviewed.
claims.heading: Hosts have alternated since 2023

sections.heading: Broader serials, constant scale
sections.intro: Official descriptions list more activities over time. The forces committed did not grow in step, and a plan announced before an exercise is not a record of what was done.

claims.text: Before the 2024 edition, China’s defence ministry said it was held under the annual plan and by mutual consensus. It listed visit, board, search and seizure among the planned activities.

event_period.date_basis: China’s ministry described the planned content on August 29, 2024, before the exercise opened.

claims.limits: This is a pre-exercise plan. It does not show who carried out the boarding serial or whether it was conducted jointly.
claims.heading: China’s 2024 plan listed boarding

claims.text: MINDEF’s pre-exercise release for 2024 said RSS Stalwart would observe PLA Navy demonstrations of boarding and mine clearance, rather than describing them as joint serials.
claims.limits: This is also a pre-exercise description. No closing account was reviewed to show what was finally conducted.
claims.heading: Singapore described an observer role

claims.text: As the 2024 edition opened, a defence-ministry account said it was longer, had more serials and involved deeper exchange than before. It described the exercise as a flagship programme of the two militaries.
claims.limits: This is a self-assessment by one participant. More listed serials and longer duration do not measure the depth of cooperation.
claims.heading: China called 2024 longer and deeper

claims.text: MINDEF’s concluding release lists sea-rider exchanges, gunnery, communications and manoeuvring drills, joint search and rescue, medical evacuation and planning exercises ashore. China’s defence ministry lists a similar set, adding replenishment at sea and live firing. PLA Daily’s opening report had listed a joint surface strike among the planned serials; neither concluding account names one.

event_period.date_basis: Both ministries report the sea phase as concluding on September 9; PLA Daily places its start on September 8.

claims.limits: Both concluding accounts are official summaries. Their silence on the planned strike serial does not show that it was dropped.
claims.heading: 2026: what the concluding accounts list

claims.text: Singapore committed one or two ships to each edition whose participants are named in the releases reviewed: two in 2015, one frigate in 2024, a frigate and a mine countermeasures vessel in 2025, and one frigate in 2026. The lists of activities lengthened; the forces did not.
claims.limits: Ship counts are an incomplete measure, and personnel numbers were not consistently available. The 2023 ship list was not checked. Publicity is not depth, and a stable force size does not show that cooperation stagnated.
claims.heading: Scale has not grown with the listed activity

sections.heading: Port calls, exchanges and meetings
sections.intro: Beyond the exercise, the record shows logistical port use, multilateral professional events and ministerial meetings. Each is narrower than its headline suggests.

claims.text: MINDEF said the PLA Navy’s 48th escort task force was at Changi Naval Base for a routine technical stop. It added that Singapore regularly facilitates transits, port calls and stopovers by foreign military ships and aircraft.

event_period.date_basis: MINDEF’s October 5 release describes the stop as under way; it gives no arrival or departure dates.

claims.limits: MINDEF presents the stop as routine and in line with its practice for many navies. Its release does not give arrival or departure dates.
claims.heading: October 2026: a technical stop at Changi

claims.text: Xinhua’s report on the task force’s October 23 return to Qingdao distinguishes friendly visits to Bangladesh, Myanmar and Malaysia from technical stops at Oman, Kenya, Singapore and other countries.
claims.limits: Both governments use the same category for the Changi call. A technical stop is a logistical port call, not a ceremonial visit or a bilateral activity.
claims.heading: China listed Singapore as a technical stop

claims.text: PLA Daily reported a PLA Navy international cadet leadership camp at Yantai that opened on August 24, 2026. Cadets from Pakistan, Indonesia, Singapore, Vietnam and other countries took part. A team from Singapore’s SAFTI Military Institute sailed in the camp’s regatta on August 25–27.

event_period.date_basis: PLA Daily dates the opening to August 24 and the regatta to August 25–27; the camp’s closing date is not given.

claims.limits: This is a multinational event hosted by China, not a bilateral exchange. Singapore’s participation is one team among several, as reported by the host.
claims.heading: August 2026: a multinational cadet camp

claims.text: PLA Daily reported that China’s defence minister Dong Jun met Singapore’s defence minister Chan Chun Sing at the Beijing Xiangshan Forum on September 16, 2026. In PLA Daily’s account, Chan called the two militaries’ cooperation in joint exercises, training and personnel development fruitful.

event_period.date_basis: PLA Daily reports the meeting on the day it took place.

claims.limits: This is the Chinese account of a Singaporean minister’s remarks. No Singaporean account of the meeting was reviewed.
claims.heading: September 2026: ministers meet in Beijing

sections.heading: Agreements and mechanisms
sections.intro: The formal framework is thin in the public record: a defence agreement of commitments, and a stated aim of regular exercising.

claims.text: A MINDEF factsheet dated October 20, 2019 describes an enhanced version of the two countries’ 2008 Agreement on Defence Exchanges and Security Cooperation. It sets out commitments for future activity.

event_period.date_basis: This is the factsheet’s publication date; the signing date was not independently checked.

claims.limits: The factsheet records commitments, not their execution. This dossier does not treat any listed commitment as carried out unless a later publication reports it.
claims.heading: 2019: an enhanced defence agreement

claims.text: In a 2023 parliamentary reply, MINDEF described Maritime Cooperation as one of two bilateral exercises with China and noted that Singapore has similar defence agreements with many countries.
claims.limits: This is Singapore’s framing for a domestic audience. It does not identify or describe the other exercise.
claims.heading: Singapore places the exercise among many

sections.heading: How each government describes it
sections.intro: The two governments describe the same activity in different registers. Neither account is independent of its author.

claims.text: Chinese state outlets describe naval cooperation with Singapore as developing in depth, increasing mutual trust and promoting practical cooperation. China’s defence ministry adds a shared ability to maintain regional peace and stability.
claims.limits: PLA Daily, the defence ministry and Xinhua are all Chinese state outlets. Agreement among them is one institution repeating itself, not corroboration.
claims.heading: China: deepening cooperation

claims.text: MINDEF presents the exercise as part of a wide network of naval partnerships and of long-standing, warm relations between the two navies. Its releases stress professional exchange rather than strategic purpose.
claims.limits: This is Singapore’s self-description; omitting strategic language is not evidence about strategic intent.
claims.heading: Singapore: one partnership among many

claims.text: In 2026 RSS Steadfast took part in RIMPAC alongside navies of 31 nations, the bilateral Singapan exercise with Japan on August 26–28 and then Maritime Cooperation at Zhanjiang. The navy also took part in an ASEAN–India maritime exercise and an ADMM-Plus maritime security exercise in late September.

event_period.date_basis: The releases date RIMPAC from June 25, Singapan to August 26–28, Maritime Cooperation to September 5–9 and the later multilateral exercises to September 21 to October 2.

claims.limits: These are Singapore’s own releases. They show the breadth of the navy’s calendar, not the relative weight Singapore gives to any one partner.
claims.heading: The same frigate, many partners

claims.text: MINDEF’s 2015 release used the word interoperability to describe the purpose of the first edition. No publication reviewed here measures interoperability or readiness, and this dossier does not claim either.
claims.limits: Stated aims are attributed to their author. Five short exercises with one or two ships a side cannot establish interoperability.
claims.heading: Interoperability is MINDEF’s word, not a finding

sections.heading: Where the record runs out
sections.intro: The public record supports a narrow finding. These limits apply to every section.

claims.text: Every source in this dossier is a publication by a Chinese or Singaporean state body. None is independent observation, and none reports operational outcomes beyond the activities each government chose to describe.
claims.limits: Matching accounts from two governments corroborate dates and participants, not quality or effect.
claims.heading: Official accounts only

claims.text: The record shows recurring, small, publicised exercising and routine port access. It does not show strategic alignment: in the same months the same Singaporean frigate exercised with the United States, Japan and others.
claims.limits: This is IPR’s interpretation. It does not exclude cooperation that is not published.
claims.heading: Exercising is not alignment

claims.text: Chinese accounts of the 2015, 2023 and 2025 editions, closing releases for 2023–2025 and any record of a 2020 edition were not reviewed. Personnel numbers are not given consistently. Absence from this dossier is not absence from the record.
claims.limits: The external research was a bounded check of linked official pages on October 26, 2026. It was not a comprehensive search.
claims.heading: What this dossier did not review

disagreements.note: Before the 2024 edition, China’s defence ministry listed boarding among the planned activities, while MINDEF described RSS Stalwart observing PLA Navy boarding and mine-clearance demonstrations. Both are pre-exercise accounts; neither settles what was conducted. Both are preserved.

China’s outlets describe deepening cooperation and a flagship programme; Singapore places the exercise within a wide network of partnerships. These are different emphases rather than contradictory facts, and this dossier does not choose between them.
